title: IND Safety Reports vs. Information Amendments vs. Protocol Amendments Under 21 CFR 312.32, 312.31 and 312.30
summary: Which submission each new nonclinical or clinical IND finding requires (IND safety report, information amendment or protocol amendment), and the deadlines for each.
body_markdown:
## IND safety reports vs. information amendments vs. protocol amendments: routing new nonclinical and clinical findings under 21 CFR 312.32, 312.31 and 312.30


### Bottom line


A new safety finding during IND development can go to FDA through up to three submissions, and each one has its own trigger:


- **IND safety report (21 CFR 312.32).** This is the expedited route. It covers serious and unexpected suspected adverse reactions, findings from other studies, findings from animal or in vitro testing that suggest a significant risk in humans, and clinically important increases in the rate of serious suspected adverse reactions. The sponsor must notify FDA and all participating investigators no later than 15 calendar days after determining that the information qualifies[35](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.32) . An unexpected fatal or life-threatening suspected adverse reaction must reach FDA within 7 calendar days of initial receipt[40](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.32) .
- **Information amendment (21 CFR 312.31).** This route carries essential IND information that falls outside a protocol amendment, an IND safety report or the annual report. Examples are new toxicology, chemistry or other technical information, and a report that a clinical investigation has been discontinued[57](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.31) . Information amendments should be submitted as necessary but, to the extent feasible, not more than every 30 days[62](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.31) .
- **Protocol amendment (21 CFR 312.30).** This route is required when a new finding leads the sponsor to change a protocol. In Phase 1 that means any change that significantly affects subject safety. In Phase 2 or 3 it also means changes that significantly affect the scope or scientific quality of the investigation[21](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.30) . The amendment must be submitted to FDA, and the IRB must approve the change, before it is implemented. The one exception is a change that eliminates an apparent immediate hazard to subjects[24](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.30)[25](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.30) .


These routes can stack. FDA's December 2025 final guidance, *Sponsor Responsibilities: Safety Reporting Requirements and Safety Assessment for IND and Bioavailability/Bioequivalence Studies* , says a finding that suggests significant risk would ordinarily lead to a safety-related change in the protocol, informed consent, investigator brochure or trial conduct. Any protocol amendment required under § 312.30(b) is submitted **in addition to** the IND safety report[326](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/ind-safety-reports-vs-information-amendments?showSourceNumber=326)[415](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/ind-safety-reports-vs-information-amendments?showSourceNumber=415) .


### Side-by-side comparison


IND safety report (§ 312.32) Information amendment (§ 312.31) Protocol amendment (§ 312.30)


Trigger Information meeting one of the four § 312.32(c)(1) categories[35](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.32) Essential information outside the scope of a protocol amendment, IND safety report or annual report[57](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.31) A new protocol, a protocol change affecting safety (any phase) or scope or scientific quality (Phase 2/3), or a new investigator[20](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.30)[21](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.30)[26](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.30)


Typical new-finding content Serious and unexpected suspected adverse reactions; significant-risk signals from other studies or from animal or in vitro testing; increased rates of serious suspected adverse reactions[36](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.32)[37](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.32)[38](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.32)[39](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.32) New toxicology, chemistry or other technical information; discontinuance of an investigation[57](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.31) Dose or exposure changes, design changes, added or dropped safety monitoring[21](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.30)[22](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.30)[23](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.30)


Timing No later than 15 calendar days after the sponsor determines the information qualifies; 7 calendar days for unexpected fatal or life-threatening suspected adverse reactions[35](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.32)[40](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.32) As necessary; to the extent feasible, not more than every 30 days[62](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.31) Before implementation, once submitted to FDA and approved by the IRB (either order); immediately if needed to eliminate an apparent immediate hazard, with FDA and the IRB notified afterward. A new-investigator amendment: notify FDA within 30 days of adding the investigator[24](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.30)[25](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.30)[33](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.30)


Recipients FDA and all participating investigators[35](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.32) FDA FDA, with IRB approval of the change[24](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.30)


Labeling "IND Safety Report"[42](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.32) For example, "Information Amendment: Pharmacology-Toxicology" or "Information Amendment: Clinical"[58](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.31) "Protocol Amendment: New Protocol / Change in Protocol / New Investigator"[27](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.30)


### When an IND safety report is required (21 CFR 312.32)


#### The four reportable categories


Under § 312.32(c)(1), the sponsor must notify FDA and all participating investigators of potential serious risks from clinical trials or any other source. Each report must identify earlier IND safety reports on similar suspected adverse reactions and analyze the new report's significance in light of them[35](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.32) . The categories are:


1. **Serious and unexpected suspected adverse reaction.** An adverse event is reported as a suspected adverse reaction only if there is evidence to suggest a causal relationship between the drug and the event[36](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.32) .
2. **Findings from other studies.** This covers epidemiological studies, pooled analyses of multiple studies, and clinical studies not already reported under (c)(1)(i), whether or not they were conducted under an IND or by the sponsor, when they suggest a significant risk in humans exposed to the drug[37](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.32) .
3. **Findings from animal or in vitro testing.** This covers results, whether or not the sponsor generated them, that suggest a significant risk in humans. The regulation gives the examples of mutagenicity, teratogenicity, carcinogenicity, and significant organ toxicity at or near the expected human exposure[38](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.32) .
4. **Increased rate of occurrence of serious suspected adverse reactions.** This covers any clinically important increase over the rate listed in the protocol or investigator brochure[39](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.32) .


#### Key definitions


- A **suspected adverse reaction** is an adverse event for which there is a reasonable possibility that the drug caused it. For IND safety reporting, "reasonable possibility" means there is evidence suggesting a causal relationship[8](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.32) .
- An event is **unexpected** if it is not listed in the investigator brochure, or is not listed at the specificity or severity observed. This includes class effects or events anticipated from the drug's pharmacology that are not specifically identified for the investigational drug[9](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.32) .
- An event is **serious** if, in the view of either the investigator or the sponsor, it results in death, a life-threatening event, inpatient or prolonged hospitalization, persistent or significant incapacity, or a congenital anomaly or birth defect. Important medical events judged to meet the standard also qualify[7](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.32) .


#### The reporting clock


The 2025 guidance defines **day zero** for both 7-day and 15-day reports in two ways. For a case that can be interpreted on its own, it is the day the sponsor first receives the information. Where multiple cases are needed, it is the day the sponsor determines that they qualify for expedited reporting[407](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/ind-safety-reports-vs-information-amendments?showSourceNumber=407) . For aggregate signals, receipt of the first event may come well before that determination[405](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/ind-safety-reports-vs-information-amendments?showSourceNumber=405) . FDA expects an uncommon single event that is strongly associated with drug exposure to be reported within 15 calendar days of initial receipt, because its reportability should be immediately apparent[408](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/ind-safety-reports-vs-information-amendments?showSourceNumber=408) . Day zero is not necessarily the date the adverse event began[409](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/ind-safety-reports-vs-information-amendments?showSourceNumber=409) .


Reports may be narrative, on Form FDA 3500A, or in an electronic format FDA can process. Foreign suspected adverse reactions may use a CIOMS I form. Reports of overall findings or pooled analyses from in vitro, animal, epidemiological or clinical studies must be narrative[41](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.32) . Under § 312.32(c)(3), a different format or frequency requires advance agreement from the director of the review division[389](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.32) .


#### Nonclinical findings: safety report or information amendment?


The dividing line is **significant risk in humans** . Animal or in vitro findings that suggest such a risk are IND safety reports under § 312.32(c)(1)(iii)[38](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.32) . FDA's guidance, in its 2012 version and carried forward in the December 2025 guidance, asks sponsors to judge whether a finding suggests significant human risk or is too preliminary to interpret without replication or further investigation[299](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/ind-safety-reports-vs-information-amendments?showSourceNumber=299) . The 2025 guidance adds that findings at exposures above clinical exposure can also warrant reporting, and gives the example of a NOAEL only marginally above clinical exposure[382](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/ind-safety-reports-vs-information-amendments?showSourceNumber=382) .


Nonclinical information that does not meet this threshold still has to reach FDA. Section 312.31 names new toxicology information as information-amendment content[57](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.31) . The annual report under § 312.33 must list preclinical studies, including animal studies, completed or in progress during the past year, with a summary of major preclinical findings[54](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.33) . In practice, completed toxicology results without a significant-risk signal go into an information amendment (labeled, for example, "Information Amendment: Pharmacology-Toxicology"[58](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.31) ) or are summarized in the annual report. A significant-risk signal requires the 15-day IND safety report.


#### Clinical findings from other studies


The 2025 guidance gives examples of significant-risk findings from other studies: results from a drug-interaction study, a QT study or a study of a marketed drug. Its specific example is significant QT prolongation in participants receiving the investigational drug[414](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/ind-safety-reports-vs-information-amendments?showSourceNumber=414) . Reporting applies whether or not the studies were run under the IND or by the sponsor[415](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/ind-safety-reports-vs-information-amendments?showSourceNumber=415) .


#### Aggregate signals and anticipated events


Anticipated serious adverse events, meaning those expected in the study population regardless of drug exposure, generally should not be reported expeditiously as individual cases. An IND safety report is required when aggregate analysis shows an imbalance between arms large enough to conclude there is a reasonable possibility the drug caused the increase[288](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/ind-safety-reports-vs-information-amendments?showSourceNumber=288)[289](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/ind-safety-reports-vs-information-amendments?showSourceNumber=289)[290](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/ind-safety-reports-vs-information-amendments?showSourceNumber=290) . The guidance describes this as a complex judgment that is almost never simply the result of a planned statistical analysis[292](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/ind-safety-reports-vs-information-amendments?showSourceNumber=292) . A data monitoring committee may make recommendations, but the reporting decision remains the sponsor's responsibility[294](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/ind-safety-reports-vs-information-amendments?showSourceNumber=294)[295](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/ind-safety-reports-vs-information-amendments?showSourceNumber=295) . Sponsors should list anticipated serious adverse events they do not plan to report individually in a surveillance plan. Leaving an anticipated event off that list does not automatically make it individually reportable[354](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/ind-safety-reports-vs-information-amendments?showSourceNumber=354) .


#### What should not go in an IND safety report


- **Events that fail the criteria.** An event should not be submitted as an IND safety report unless it is serious, unexpected and supported by evidence suggesting a causal relationship[357](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/ind-safety-reports-vs-information-amendments?showSourceNumber=357) . A positive causality assessment from the investigator alone is not enough when the sponsor finds no such evidence[358](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/ind-safety-reports-vs-information-amendments?showSourceNumber=358) . Events that do not meet the criteria must still be reported under the periodic-reporting regulations, such as the IND annual report[359](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/ind-safety-reports-vs-information-amendments?showSourceNumber=359) .
- **Study endpoints.** Endpoints such as mortality or major morbidity are reported as the protocol describes and ordinarily not as IND safety reports. The exception is a serious and unexpected event with evidence of a causal relationship, which must be reported under (c)(1)(i) even if it is part of the endpoint. The regulation's example is death from anaphylaxis counted within an all-cause mortality endpoint[14](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.32) .


#### Follow-up information


Relevant follow-up information is submitted as soon as available as a "Followup IND Safety Report." If an event first judged nonreportable is later found to be reportable, the IND safety report is due within 15 calendar days of that determination[12](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.32)[13](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.32) . FDA's guidance, in its 2012 version and carried forward in the 2025 guidance, says additional information that is *not* relevant to evaluating the suspected adverse reaction is kept in sponsor records and, if applicable, submitted in an information amendment or the annual report[360](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/ind-safety-reports-vs-information-amendments?showSourceNumber=360) .


#### Studies of marketed drugs


For IND studies of drugs marketed or approved in the United States, sponsors submit IND safety reports for suspected adverse reactions at domestic or foreign study sites. They also submit study safety information under the postmarketing safety reporting requirements, such as §§ 310.305, 314.80 and 600.80[390](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.32) .


### When an information amendment is the right vehicle (21 CFR 312.31)


Section 312.31 is the catch-all for essential IND information that does not belong in a protocol amendment, an IND safety report or the annual report[57](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.31) . Each submission must identify its contents prominently[58](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.31) and contain:


- a statement of the nature and purpose of the amendment[59](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.31) ;
- an organized submission of data in a format suitable for scientific review[60](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.31) ; and
- a request for FDA comment, if the sponsor wants it[61](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.31) .


The timing is flexible: as necessary but, to the extent feasible, not more than every 30 days[62](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.31) . When a safety-driven protocol change depends on new technical data, § 312.30(d) allows the protocol amendment to reference supporting information in the IND or in an information amendment submitted at the same time[31](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.30) .


### When a protocol amendment is required (21 CFR 312.30)


A new safety finding becomes a protocol-amendment issue once the sponsor decides to change how the study is run. Section 312.30(b) gives these examples:


- increasing dose or duration of exposure beyond the current protocol, or significantly increasing the number of subjects[21](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.30) ;
- significant design changes, such as adding or dropping a control group[22](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.30) ; and
- adding a test or procedure to improve monitoring for, or reduce the risk of, a side effect or adverse event, or dropping a safety-monitoring test[23](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.30) .


Such changes may be implemented only after the amendment has been submitted to FDA and the IRB has approved it, in either order[24](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.30) . A change intended to eliminate an apparent immediate hazard to subjects may be implemented immediately. FDA is then notified by protocol amendment and the IRB is notified in accordance with § 56.104(c)[25](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.30) . Each amendment must briefly describe the change and give the date and number of the submission that contained the protocol[29](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.30) .


FDA's guidance lists the kinds of protocol changes that typically follow a significant-risk finding: immediate revision of informed consent, more intensive monitoring, revised eligibility or screening criteria, an enrollment hold, or consideration of stopping the trial[415](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/ind-safety-reports-vs-information-amendments?showSourceNumber=415) . For oncology master protocols, FDA's 2022 guidance says protocol amendments under § 312.30 should include the revised consent documents. Where an immediate-hazard change has already been made, the revised consent should be submitted as soon as possible[336](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/ind-safety-reports-vs-information-amendments?showSourceNumber=336) .


### Related obligations triggered by the same finding


- **Investigator brochure.** FDA's 2012 guidance, withdrawn in December 2025, said a significant risk should be communicated to investigators immediately, together with an investigator brochure update and possibly a protocol change. A minor change in the rate of a suspected adverse reaction may be updated annually instead[327](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/ind-safety-reports-vs-information-amendments?showSourceNumber=327) . Until a new serious suspected adverse reaction is added to the brochure, similar later occurrences must continue to be reported as IND safety reports[329](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/ind-safety-reports-vs-information-amendments?showSourceNumber=329) .
- **Informing investigators (§ 312.55(b)).** Sponsors must keep investigators informed of new observations, particularly about adverse effects and safe use, and relay important safety information in accordance with § 312.32[45](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.55) .
- **Unreasonable and significant risk (§ 312.56(d)).** If the drug presents an unreasonable and significant risk to subjects, the sponsor must discontinue the investigations that present the risk as soon as possible, and no later than 5 working days after deciding to stop. The sponsor must also notify FDA, all IRBs and all investigators who ever participated, and send FDA a full report of its actions[46](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.56) . A report regarding discontinuance is also listed as information-amendment content[57](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.31) .
- **Annual report (§ 312.33).** Due within 60 days of the IND anniversary[48](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.33) , the annual report must include a narrative or tabular summary of the most frequent and most serious adverse experiences by body system[50](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.33) , a summary of all IND safety reports submitted during the past year[51](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.33) , deaths with cause[52](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.33) , dropouts associated with adverse experiences[53](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.33) , and preclinical findings[54](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.33) . FDA's 2012 guidance, withdrawn in December 2025, said FDA accepts the ICH E2F Development Safety Update Report as meeting the annual report requirement[361](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/ind-safety-reports-vs-information-amendments?showSourceNumber=361) . Sponsors relying on a DSUR should confirm the current conditions in FDA's ICH E2F guidance. The annual report summarizes earlier IND safety reports; it does not replace a qualifying expedited report[387](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/ind-safety-reports-vs-information-amendments?showSourceNumber=387) .


### Practical routing guide

### Points that often cause errors


- **The 15-day clock runs from the reportability determination, not from event onset.** Sponsors still cannot delay assessing a case. Incomplete cases must be followed up promptly[408](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/ind-safety-reports-vs-information-amendments?showSourceNumber=408)[409](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/ind-safety-reports-vs-information-amendments?showSourceNumber=409)[11](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.32) .
- **"Significant risk" is the test for nonclinical findings and findings from other studies.** A finding that would ordinarily lead to a safety-related protocol, consent or investigator brochure change, not just a routine update, is the practical marker FDA describes[415](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/ind-safety-reports-vs-information-amendments?showSourceNumber=415) .
- **Overreporting is a compliance problem too.** Single, uninformative cases of events common in the population, or of disease-related outcomes, generally lack evidence of causality and should not be submitted as IND safety reports[352](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/ind-safety-reports-vs-information-amendments?showSourceNumber=352) .
- **A safety report does not admit causation.** Under § 312.32(e), submitting a safety report does not necessarily reflect a conclusion by the sponsor or FDA that the drug caused or contributed to the adverse event[15](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.32) .
